result.summary: Ligdus orders his wife Telethusa to kill a baby girl, but Isis tells her in a dream to raise the child. Telethusa raises the girl as a boy named Iphis, who is betrothed to Ianthe and despairs of the match. On the eve of the wedding Isis answers Telethusa's prayer and turns Iphis into a man.

scenes.title: Ligdus's cruel command
scenes.summary: Ligdus, a poor but honest man of Phaestus, tells his pregnant wife to kill any daughter. Both weep, and she begs in vain.
scenes.stakes: Telethusa's unborn child may be killed if it is a girl.

scenes.title: Isis's dream and Iphis's birth
scenes.summary: Isis appears to Telethusa with her retinue and tells her to raise the child. A girl is born and raised as a boy under the name Iphis.
scenes.stakes: The newborn girl's life and Telethusa's secret.

scenes.title: Iphis's despair for Ianthe
scenes.summary: At thirteen Iphis is betrothed to Ianthe, and the two fall in love. Iphis laments that her passion is unnatural and that no god or craftsman can help.
scenes.stakes: Iphis faces a marriage she cannot fulfil and a love that nature forbids.

scenes.title: Isis transforms Iphis
scenes.summary: Telethusa runs out of delaying excuses and prays at Isis's altar. The goddess signals her favour, Iphis becomes a man on the way home, and the wedding takes place.
scenes.stakes: Exposure of the deception on the wedding day.

alias_notes.explanation: Ovid identifies Isis with Io, daughter of the river-god Inachus.

notable_quotes.reason: Iphis's vivid image of longing: thirst in the midst of water.
The dedicatory inscription neatly sums up the transformation.

analysis.text: The story explores desire, nature and deception, with divine pity overcoming a cruel parental order and a love nature forbids.
It reflects the Roman vogue for Isis cult and the ancient practice of exposing unwanted girls.

legacy.text: Ovid's tale of Iphis and Ianthe has been retold by later writers, including Gower, and is often discussed in studies of gender and sexuality in literature.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's Iphis is one of few Metamorphoses transformations that goes from female to male; most of the others go the other way.

language_notes.text: Crete was proverbially 'hundred-citied'; the 'new prodigy' is Iphis's change of sex, which the narrator is about to tell, a nearer wonder than the earlier one.
Phæstian means of Phaestus, a city in southern Crete; Gnossian refers to Gnossus (Knossos), the royal city of King Minos.
'Startled the ears' means he shocked her by speaking; 'lying-in' is the old term for confinement during childbirth.
'The other alternative' means having a girl; 'providence' here means fate or the gods, who have left the couple too poor to raise a daughter.
'Natural affection' is addressed directly, as if asking parental love to forgive the order. Ligdus is commanding exposure or killing of a female infant.
"Daughter of Inachus" is a periphrasis for Isis, identified with Io, the daughter of the river-god Inachus whom Jupiter loved and Juno transformed into a cow.
The figures are Egyptian deities in Isis's train: dog-headed Anubis, cat-goddess Bubastis, the sacred bull Apis, and Harpocrates, the god of silence, who holds his finger to his lips.
Sistra are rattles shaken in the worship of Isis.
Lucina is the goddess of childbirth, often identified with Juno or Diana.
"Evade the commands of thy husband" refers to Ligdus's order to kill any daughter born. Here, the husband's command is to be disobeyed.
"The father unaware of it" means Ligdus did not know the child was a girl, because the mother and nurse hid the fact.
Iphis is a name that can belong to either a man or a woman, so using it is not strictly a lie.
'The third year had succeeded the tenth' means Iphis was thirteen.
Phæstus and Dictæan refer to Crete: Phæstus was a Cretan city, and Mount Dicte was also in Crete.
The daughter of the Sun is Pasiphaë, wife of Minos, who loved a bull and bore the Minotaur.
Pasiphaë hid inside a wooden cow made by Dædalus to mate with the bull.
Dædalus escaped Crete by flying on wings of feathers fastened with wax; his son Icarus fell when the wax melted.
Proverbial image like Tantalus's torment: she is surrounded by what she wants yet cannot have it.
Juno presided over marriage and Hymenæus was the god of wedding songs; both are called to a wedding that cannot be proper.
Fillets are ribbons or headbands for the hair. Removing them and loosening her hair shows suppliant humility and distress.
Parætonium, the Mareotic fields, Pharos and the Nile's seven mouths are Egyptian sites sacred to Isis, so Telethusa invokes the goddess through her homeland.
Sistra are rattles of metal rods on a frame, shaken in Isis worship; her torches and attendants were also part of her cult.
Refers to Isis's earlier dream-command to raise the baby girl despite her husband's order to kill any daughter, so Telethusa was not punished.
Isis was shown with cow's horns, or a crescent moon, on her head; the shining horns signal her presence and favour.
Venus, Juno and Hymenæus were the deities of love, marriage and the wedding song; their presence marks a proper, blessed wedding.

context_notes.text: 'Freeborn' marks Ligdus as a free citizen, neither slave nor noble, so his poverty is respectable rather than shameful.
In the ancient Greek world, poor families sometimes killed or exposed unwanted infants, girls more often than boys, because dowries and upkeep were costly.
Telethusa is a Cretan woman. Her husband Ligdus has ordered that a daughter be put to death, which is why she needs the goddess's help.
Isis was an Egyptian goddess whose worship spread across the Roman world. She was known as a helper of women and of those who prayed to her.
Naming a child after the grandfather was a common custom. The father also performs vows of thanks for what he believes is a son.
Iphis was born a girl but raised as a boy by her mother, to hide her sex from her father, who had ordered a daughter killed.
Iphis speaks in a soliloquy, seeing her desire as unnatural and with no precedent, even in myth.
Iphis was raised as a boy and betrothed to Iänthe, so the wedding would expose the secret that Iphis is a girl.
Shaking altars and doors were standard signs that a god had heard a prayer.
Dedicating a votive offering with an inscription was a customary way to repay a vow to a god.

literary_notes.text: The narrator gives Ligdus poverty but spotless honour, so the reader sees his cruel order as coming from necessity, not wickedness.
Ligdus turns to 'natural affection' as if it were a person, showing his inner conflict as he gives the order.
Both spouses weeping, the commander as much as the commanded, deepens the sorrow and shows the order is a grief to both.
The blunt statement that his resolve is fixed sets up the tension that the gods will have to resolve.
"Either stood, or seemed to stand" shows the narrator's hedging over the vision, balancing dream against real divine presence.
A catalogue of vivid emblems, such as the moon's horns, golden grain and a crown, presents Isis's divine majesty and the strangeness of her foreign cult.
The deception is called a "fraud" yet is prompted by "natural affection", so a lie is shown as an act of love.
Iphis lists animals to show that her desire has no parallel in nature, deepening her isolation.
Repeating 'Hope it is' stresses hope as the sustaining force of love, which she lacks.
Being thirsty amid water compresses her predicament into one image: the object of desire is near but unattainable.
Telethusa dreads what she desires: she wants the marriage to happen yet fears what it will reveal, capturing her divided mind.
The parenthetical assertion that the goddess really moved the altars is the narrator vouching for the miracle.
Quick, piled-up clauses about stride, face, strength and hair make the transformation seem to occur step by step as they walk.
The narrator suddenly addresses Iphis directly, marking the change with immediacy and sympathy.
Morning is said to uncover the world with the sun's rays, while the gods themselves attend the wedding, giving a bright, joyous close.
